In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of protein phosphorylation in the regulation of starch biosynthesis in maize endosperms.
the role of starch biosynthetic enzyme complexes in the control of starch biosynthesis in maize endosperms.
the identification of protein-protein interaction in starch synthesizing complexes and their role in the biosynthesis of starch.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amylose extender mutation of maize results in the absence of SBEIIa activity and that this results in a change in the protein-protein interactions that occur within amyloplasts.

the loss of the SBEIIb isoform results in novel protein complexes in maize endosperms amyloplasts that are not phosphorylated dependent and that these novel complexes have a functional role in amylopectins biosynthesis.
the ae mutant of maize is a model for understanding the functional complementation of starch branching enzyme II activity by other starch branching enzyme isoforms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in maize endosperms, the amylose extender mutation conditions the formation of novel protein complexes in the amyloplasts that contain starch biosynthetic proteins, and these complexes may play an important role in amylopecti biosynthesis.

the ae(-) mutant of maize conditions a novel phosphorylation dependent protein-protein interaction in the amyloplast that involves SBEI, SP and SSIIa, in place of the SBEIIb interaction in the wild type.

the amylose extender mutants of maize have novel protein-protein interaction patterns between starch biosynthesizing enzymes in amylopectins, and that these interactions are dependent on phosphorylation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amylose extender mutants of maize provide a useful model system for investigating the functional significance of protein-protein complexes in starch biosynthesis.

the loss of one of the starch synthase enzymes, SBEIIb in this case, can lead to the reprogramming of the other starch synthase enzymes in the cell to compensate for the lost function, which in turn leads to the formation of new protein complexes that are different from those that are formed in wild-type cells.
